background.definition: Pain in the knee caused by damage to cartilage, inflammation, infection, or injury. The focus of this chapter is on nontraumatic knee pain.

list.listitem: In 2006, nearly 1 in 5 adults had self-reported, doctor-diagnosed arthritis.
Over $81 billion in medical costs in 2003; cost to US economy $128 billion annually.
Leading cause of disability in the United States; 36 million physician visits and 750,000 hospitalizations annually.
Limits activities of daily living for 19 million Americans.
Osteoarthritis is the most common cause in persons 45 years and older.
Crystal-induced arthritides (eg, gout, pseudogout)
Patellofemoral pain syndrome
Rheumatic arthritides
Septic arthritis
Crystal-induced arthritis (eg, gout, pseudogout ): Pain is due to inflammation from crystal deposition.

Osteoarthritis: Pain is due to biomechanical and biochemical forces. Cytokines, interleukin-1, tumor necrosis factor-β, collagenase 1, collagenase 2, and collagenase 3 may play a role in cartilage degeneration. Pain may be mechanical (weight-bearing) and/or inflammatory.
Patellofemoral syndrome: Pain is partially mechanical, often due to positions or activities that load the patella. In some cases, the pain is also due to inflammation.
Rheumatoid arthritis: Pain is due to inflammation from autoimmune processes.
Septic arthritis: Pain is due to joint infection, from wound, spread from adjacent soft tissue infection, or hematogenous spread of osteomyelitis.

In a small study of young patients (ages 11-25 years), those with idiopathic anterior knee pain had statistically significant hamstring tightness and increased external hip rotation compared to a control group.

list.listitem: Diagnostic criteria for osteoarthritis, gout, and rheumatoid arthritis are shown in the chapters for those conditions.
Distinguishing between traumatic and nontraumatic knee pain helps narrow the differential diagnosis.
Most patients older than 50 years with knee pain have osteoarthritis. Most patients younger than 50 years have patellofemoral pain syndrome.

Patients with knee osteoarthritis typically have osseous hypertrophy (LR+ 3.3, LR- 0.6) and may have joint line tenderness medially or laterally. Pain is worse with activity or prolonged standing and improves with rest. Unlike collagen vascular diseases that cause knee pain, it is typically better in the morning and worsens as the day goes.

A study of 279 patients with knee pain diagnosed patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) in 75. PFPS was more likely in patients younger than 40 years with isolated anterior knee pain or medial patellar facet tenderness (64% sensitive, 93% specific, LR+ 8.7), as well as in patients 40 to 58 years with isolated anterior or diffuse knee pain, mild to moderate difficulty descending stairs, medial patellar facet tenderness, and full passive knee extension (56% sensitive, 96% specific, LR+ 14.3). Anterior knee pain is 92% sensitive and 50% specific (LR+ 1.8, LR- .16) so its absence makes the diagnosis significantly less likely. The diagnosis was unlikely in patients under 58 years with medial, lateral or posterior knee pain and no medial or lateral patellar facet tenderness (LR- 0.12), and in patients under 58 years with diffuse or lateral knee pain, medial or lateral patellar facet tenderness, and restricted passive knee extension (LR- 0.005) or in any patients age 58 years or older.

In a study of 255 patients with knee trauma, each was examined independently by 2 orthopedic surgeons at time 1 (5-7 days post-injury) and time 2 (4 to 5 weeks post-injury). They were blinded to MRI and history. The McMurray test was 91% sensitive and 55% specific at T1 (LR+ 2.0, LR- 0.16) and 80% sensitive and 79% specific at T2 (LR+ 3.8, LR- 0.25). Joint line tenderness is 83% sensitive and specific for meniscal injury.

Aspirate a swollen knee that is warm or erythematous and send the fluid for cell count, crystals, and culture. Independent risk factors for septic arthritis in adults include duration of pain >2 days, history of septic arthritis in any joint, and presence of a clinically detectable effusion. A clinical diagnosis of gout is appropriate without fluid aspiration unless septic joint is suspected.
See Knee Injury (Ligamentous) for discussion of diagnosis of meniscal and ligamentous injuries. Clinical factors can modestly predict menisceal tears in primary care settings.
For diagnosis of ACL injury, the anterior drawer and Lachman tests are most accurate. They are very specific but less sensitive than MRI.
In patients with nondiagnostic examination, consider imaging, aspiration, blood testing and/or referral to determine the etiology.

For a warm, swollen, erythematous joint, aspirate the fluid. Use to guide interpretation of the fluid. Septic arthritis requires an urgent response since the joint can be destroyed by the infectious process.
Procalcitonin > 0.25 ng/ml was 92% sensitive and 55% specific for septic arthritis (LR+ 2.0, LR- 0.15). A cutoff > 0.32 ng/ml was 79% sensitive and 72% specific (LR+ 2.8, LR- 0.29).

For patients without red flags or swelling, an initial trial of rest and NSAIDs is appropriate. If no response, initial imaging should include standing AP and lateral radiographs; consider tangential view of the patella-femoral joint ("sunrise" view) and a standing PA view taken in 40 degrees of flexion in younger patients when patellofemoral syndrome is suspected.
Joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis are common in persons with osteoarthritis of the knee(s).
For knee pain with nondiagnostic physical examination, aspiration results, and imaging, consider blood testing (eg, uric acid, CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies).

MRI should not replace an experienced examination; therefore, consider referral if either examination or MRI is nondiagnostic. In fact, meniscal tears are often seen on MRI in asymptomatic patients. In one cohort study, meniscal tears were seen on MRI in 32% of men and 19% of women between the ages of 50 and 59 years and 56% of men and 51% of women between the ages of 70 and 90 years; most (61%) were seen in patients without symptoms in the past month. One study found MRI useful in diagnosing more severe grades (II, III, or IV) of chondromalacia patellae.
Ultrasound is under investigation for the diagnosis of crystal arthropathy and can detect joint effusion, synovial hypertrophy and crystal deposition in the knee joint and knee soft tissue.
American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria (updated 2019) are summarized below:
Acute knee pain, fall or acute twisting trauma: initial imaging with radiography, CT without IV contrast may be appropriate if no fracture seen on radiographs.

Chronic knee pain: initial imaging is radiography. If radiography negative or joint effusion, options include aspiration of the knee, CT or MR arthrography. If initial imaging shows osteochondiritis dissecans, loose bodies, or history of cartilage or meniscal repair, MRI is appropriate.
Chronic knee pain with degenerative changes or chondrocalcinosis on radiograph, consider MRI without contrast, CT without contrast, or knee aspiration depending on clinical scenario.
See the algorithm in for a suggested approach to the patient presenting with nontraumatic knee pain. Refer to the Knee Injury chapter for patients with an acute injury to the knee.

In patients with nontraumatic knee pain, assess for swelling. Aspirate knees with inflammatory swelling (even slight warmth or erythema) to determine the etiology and ensure there is no infection. Suspect other causes of knee pain when examination, imaging, and/or aspiration are nondiagnostic.

Following a physical examination for nontraumatic knee pain, a knee x-ray is recommended for children and adolescents with anterior patellofemoral or nonpatellofemoral symptoms and for adults with nonlocalized knee pain. If the initial radiograph in adults shows degenerative joint disease or chondrocalcinosis or inflammatory or crystalline disease, no further imaging is recommended.

If the initial radiograph is nondiagnostic in these categories, an MRI is recommended. An MRI is also recommended in children and adolescents with nonpatellofemoral symptoms where the initial radiograph shows osteochondral injuries and for adults when initial radiographs demonstrate avascular necrosis or internal derangement.

The typical patient with osteoarthritis has unilateral or bilateral pain, sometimes swelling, and sometimes decreased range of motion. Usually the pain is gradual in onset. Occasionally, there may be abrupt onset with injury. Pain may occur with weight-bearing activity and at the end of the day. X-rays, often normal, may also demonstrate decreased joint space, osteophytes, or subchondral cyst formation. In a 1-year follow-up study, knee joint space narrowing progressed similarly (0.2 mm/year) regardless of baseline narrowing.

The typical patient with patellofemoral syndrome presents with gradual onset of peripatellar pain; unilateral or bilateral pain; and/or pain with flexed knee (stairs, sitting, running). Biomechanical issues are common (patellar tracking); one study found an increased lateral condyle-patella angle (increased medial patella inclination) was associated with less knee pain. The diagnosis is made clinically.

In one study, a telephone-screening questionnaire was found useful for detecting symptomatic knee and hip OA; sensitivity for knee OA was 87% (95% CI, 79%-95%) and specificity was 92% (95% CI, 91%-93%) (LR+ 10.9, LR− 0.14).
Further work-up is needed in patients with nocturnal/unremitting pain, systemic symptoms (fevers, chills, weight loss), significant disability, or change in normal ability.

Diagnose rheumatic arthritides and refer promptly as early treatment can improve prognosis. A clinical prediction rule has been developed and validated that predicts the likelihood of rheumatoid arthritis at 1 year in patients presenting with joint pain.

feature.caption: Classification of Joint Fluid from Aspiration.
feature.feature_body:
Type of Fluid Color/Quality Count (mm3)
Normal Clear, viscous <200 WBCs
Noninflammatory Clear, viscous, yellow 200-2000 WBCs
Crystal-induced Cloudy with crystals 2000-5000 WBCs with crystals
Inflammatory Cloudy, decreased viscosity, yellow 5000-50,000 WBCs
Septic Purulent, markedly decreased viscosity >50,000 WBCs (>95% polymorphonuclear leukocytes) (bacteria on gram stain, positive culture)
